title: Gargi's questions
word: in their own words where they exist
hook: warned 'don't ask too much, or your head will fall off', Gargi comes back with two questions, and the answer is Brahman
carry: everything is woven on brahman, the imperishable
tomorrow: Maitreyi asks what wealth can't buy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Lal Ded: too much gets you nowhere, too little makes you proud, and in measure the doors open.

Don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. That's a line from an Upanishad, said in a king's hall in front of learned men, to a woman who wouldn't stop asking questions. Her name is Gargi, and you first met her back in year two. She falls silent. And later, in the same debate, she stands up again. Akka and Lalla left sayings of their own. Other women's words didn't survive at all. And some, like Gargi's, speak inside a text that's mostly about someone else. Where their words exist, we listen.
screen: `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH.` → `A WOMAN WHO KEEPS ASKING.` → `HER WORDS INSIDE ANOTHER STORY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. King Janaka of Videha has called the wise to his court, and the sage Yajnavalkya is answering all comers. Gargi steps forward. Her question, in paraphrase: all this world is woven back and forth on water, like threads on a loom. So on what is water woven? On wind, he says. And wind? On the sky. Layer after layer, each answer becomes her next question. Then Yajnavalkya stops her: Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. And she falls silent. It's easy to stop there, as if she lost. The text doesn't. Later she rises again and tells the assembly: I will ask him two questions. The Upanishad pictures her like a warrior stringing a bow and taking up two arrows. That which is above the sky and below the earth, and between them, past, present and future: on what is it woven? In space, he answers. And space, on what is that woven? This time he names what's under everything: the imperishable, which the wise call Brahman. It sees and is not seen, hears and is not heard. Gargi tells the assembly none of them will beat him. That's one of the great teachings of the Upanishads: under every layer of the world is one reality, Brahman, and everything is woven on it. And notice how it arrived. Not as a decree. As the answer to a woman's questions. The Upanishads teach by asking.
screen: `A DEBATE IN KING JANAKA'S HALL` · `ON WHAT IS IT WOVEN?` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH` · `TWO ARROWS: THE IMPERISHABLE, BRAHMAN`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a cup, a hand, the floor, and ask quietly, the way the Upanishads ask: on what is this woven? What holds it up? Let an answer come, then ask the same of that answer. When you reach the place where no answer comes, don't push; rest there in the question, the way Gargi did when she fell silent. If you pray, rest there before God.
In their own words, where they exist: Gargi, warned not to ask too much, who came back with two questions like arrows. Today's word.
Your line: everything is woven on Brahman, the imperishable. A warning didn't end her questions. See you tomorrow.

Janaka.meaning: king of Videha, who called the wise to his court

notes: Max Müller's 1884 translation of the Brihadaranyaka (SBE 15) is public domain, but its exact wording could not be verified, so everything is paraphrased.

BU 3.6: confirm the chain (water, wind/air, sky/atmosphere, onward) and the warning, which the text gives as 'do not ask too much, lest your head fall off', about a deity not to be asked about too much.

BU 3.8: confirm the warrior of Kashi or Videha image, the two questions (above the sky, below the earth, between, past/present/future: on what woven?), the answers (space; the imperishable, akshara) and Gargi's verdict that none will defeat him.
